section_summary: This section documents the Allied effort to obtain custody of former Japanese diplomatic and consular archives, property, and funds held by protecting powers in neutral countries after Japan’s surrender. It includes policy discussions and operational reports from Europe and Latin America, particularly a dispute with the Japanese Consulate General in Dublin and completed transfers in Argentina and Chile. Extensive protocols, financial records, and inventories describe the assets transferred and the continuing role of the Swiss and Swedish legations in protecting Japanese nationals.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the French aide-mémoire concerning Japanese property
subfiles.from: John C. H. Bonbright, Department of State
subfiles.about: Discusses French participation in handling Japanese archives in Beirut and Japanese property outside Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum forwards the French aide-mémoire of September 24 and urges a decision after six weeks of delay. It favors including France both in the Beirut archive question and in broader discussions of Japanese property, despite an earlier policy established by Assistant Secretary Holmes.

subfiles.title: Telegram 1363 from Bogotá on Japanese archives, property, and funds
subfiles.about: Requests instructions for Allied acquisition or disposition of Japanese archives, legation property, and blocked funds in Colombia.
subfiles.summary: The American, British, and Soviet representatives propose jointly inviting the Swiss Chargé to transfer the Japanese archives and property. They seek guidance on the costly legation lease, furniture, blocked funds totaling about 90,000 pesos, support for indigent Japanese nationals, and their lack of personnel competent to examine the archives. Wiley suggests that the Colombian government might instead hold everything while guaranteeing Allied access.

subfiles.title: Telegram 2824 from Buenos Aires on transfer preparations
subfiles.about: Reports Swiss readiness to transfer former Japanese Embassy property and archives to Allied representatives.
subfiles.summary: The Swiss Legation has received instructions to surrender the property and archives, and the American and British embassies expect to take possession the following week. The Swiss intend to retain Tani or another Japanese national for language work and may require occasional access to the records while continuing routine protection work.

subfiles.title: Special Projects Division memorandum revising the Bogotá telegram
subfiles.from: Robert E. Hibbard, Special Projects Division
subfiles.about: Notes that a draft reply to Bogotá telegram 1363 was rewritten in the Special Projects Division.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies the underlying Foreign Activity Correlation draft concerning Bogotá’s November 9 telegram. It records that the proposed reply was rewritten by the Special Projects Division.

subfiles.title: Outgoing telegram to Bogotá on custody and expenses
subfiles.about: Provides instructions on the Japanese legation lease, archives, furniture, and blocked funds in Colombia.
subfiles.summary: The Department approves the proposed joint approach but refuses to authorize renewal of the Japanese legation lease. It directs that the archives remain available for examination and Swiss protection work, while the Swiss Chargé, Allied representatives, and Colombian Foreign Office negotiate the use of blocked funds and account for protection expenditures.

subfiles.title: Unsent draft telegram to Bogotá
subfiles.about: Offers an alternative proposed response on Colombian custody, archive access, and protection expenses.
subfiles.summary: The unsent draft states that the Department wishes to avoid expenses and primarily cares about the records and archives. It recommends following Bogotá’s suggestion of Colombian custody if access is assured and leaving the blocked-funds question to the Swiss Chargé and Colombian Foreign Office.

subfiles.title: Telegram 4691 from Bern
subfiles.about: Provides a brief cross-reference concerning the status of Japanese records and property in Switzerland.
subfiles.summary: The surviving text refers to Bern telegram 4689 and Department telegram 3189 of November 2. The substantive message is largely absent or illegible on the page.

subfiles.title: Outgoing telegram 3261 to Bern requesting a status report
subfiles.about: Asks Bern to report the current status of Japanese records and property.
subfiles.summary: The Department explains that Japan issued telegraphic instructions to its missions abroad on October 31 pursuant to General MacArthur’s directive. It asks the legation to report on the present condition of the records-and-property matter in Switzerland.

subfiles.title: Outgoing telegram 1017 to Lima
subfiles.about: Clarifies that MacArthur’s directive permits continued Swedish protection functions and urges notification of Peru’s Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: The Department responds to Lima telegram 1137 by pointing to provisions for Swedish protection work in the October 23 circular. It states that the Foreign Office should be notified as soon as possible.

subfiles.title: Telegram 1378 from Brussels on whether France was included
subfiles.about: Seeks clarification of France’s status under MacArthur’s directive on Japanese diplomatic property and archives.
subfiles.summary: The British Embassy questions whether the directive correctly names France among countries receiving direct custody of Japanese diplomatic and consular property. Brussels asks whether France should instead participate only through the four-power Allied procedure.

subfiles.title: Telegram 2097 from Cairo on projected transfer
subfiles.about: Reports that the Swiss Minister expects to transfer Japanese property and archives around December 1.
subfiles.summary: The Swiss Minister informally states that he will be ready for the transfer at the beginning of December. Representatives of the other three powers are coordinating to receive the material at that time.

subfiles.title: Despatch 463 transmitting Vatican correspondence
subfiles.about: Transmits Vatican, American, and British correspondence concerning Japanese archives and property at the Holy See.
subfiles.summary: Tittmann forwards the Holy See’s November 8 note and its translation. He also encloses the American note verbale of August 31 and the British communication of November 1 on the Japanese mission to the Holy See.

subfiles.title: Holy See note 108217 and English translation
subfiles.from: Secretariat of State of His Holiness
subfiles.about: Reports the Japanese delegate’s response to Allied instructions concerning Japanese diplomats in neutral countries.
subfiles.summary: The Holy See states that its Japanese Special Delegate knows of MacArthur’s communications to the Japanese government. Japan reportedly asked American authorities for an explanation because it believed the demands inconsistent with the Potsdam agreement, and the delegate had received no further instructions.

subfiles.title: Note verbale 477 concerning the Japanese Embassy to the Holy See
subfiles.from: Assistant to the Personal Representative of the U.S. President to the Pope
subfiles.to: Secretariat of State of His Holiness
subfiles.about: Warns against destruction or removal of Japanese Embassy archives pending formal surrender instructions.
subfiles.summary: The note explains that Japanese missions in neutral countries will be ordered to relinquish diplomatic and consular property and archives to Allied custody. It asks that the responsible Japanese official in Vatican City preserve the Embassy archives and notes British and Chinese support for the approach.

subfiles.title: British note on MacArthur’s instructions to the Japanese mission
subfiles.from: Sir D’Arcy Osborne, British Minister to the Holy See
subfiles.to: Secretariat of State of His Holiness
subfiles.about: Asks whether the Japanese representative has received MacArthur’s recall and property-transfer instructions.
subfiles.summary: The note cites MacArthur’s October 21 directions to transfer Japanese diplomatic and consular property and archives to Allied representatives. It also cites the order recalling Japanese representatives from neutral countries and requests confirmation of receipt.

subfiles.title: Telegram 1137 from Lima
subfiles.about: Reports disagreement over Swedish funds and plans to open Japanese safes in Lima.
subfiles.summary: Pao argues that continued Swedish control of Japanese local-currency funds and protection work conflicts with MacArthur’s termination of Japanese foreign relations, while Roberts favors resolving the issue before notifying the Foreign Office. The embassy asks for guidance and reports that the safes may have to be drilled open, risking damage to their contents.

subfiles.title: Duplicate outgoing telegram 1017 to Lima
subfiles.about: Directs Lima to recognize Swedish protection functions and notify the Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: The Department reiterates that MacArthur’s directive permits the Swedes to perform protection functions. It urges prompt notification of the Foreign Office.

subfiles.title: Telegram 6562 from Paris
subfiles.about: Reports arrangements for transferring Japanese diplomatic property and archives to French custody.
subfiles.summary: The Swiss Legation expects to transfer custody to the French government during the week, after consultation with the French, British, Chinese, and American representatives. The French Foreign Office will arrange Allied examination and access but doubts the files contain much of interest because Swiss custody began only in February 1945.

subfiles.title: Telegram 219 from Dublin on the first demand to the Japanese consul
subfiles.about: Describes the unsuccessful attempt to summon the Japanese Consul General and obtain records and property.
subfiles.summary: American and British representatives prepared a joint memorandum instructing the Japanese Consul General to appear at the American Consulate General with information, keys, and records. The consul did not comply, and Gray refers to a follow-up joint telegram and a forthcoming detailed despatch.

subfiles.title: Telegram 3851 from Moscow on delivering MacArthur’s directive
subfiles.about: Explains why the embassy withheld a delayed, isolated presentation of MacArthur’s directive to the Soviet Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: The directive on Japanese diplomatic and consular property reached Moscow more than two weeks after its issuance. Believing a full set had already been furnished to the Soviet Embassy in Washington, the embassy feared that presenting the isolated directive would arouse suspicion and deferred delivery pending further instructions.

subfiles.title: Telegram to SCAP quoting the Allied memorandum to the Dublin consul
subfiles.about: Transmits the full text of the Allied memorandum demanding records, assets, keys, and personnel information from the Japanese Consul General in Dublin.
subfiles.summary: The quoted memorandum summons the consul to the American Consulate General and lists eleven categories of documents and information required for the transfer. These include leases, automobile registrations, bank books, asset data, keys, inventories, and lists of Japanese residents and consular employees.

subfiles.title: Telegram to SCAP quoting Dublin telegram 233
subfiles.about: Reports the Dublin consul’s renewed refusal to comply fully and recommends stronger instructions from Japan.
subfiles.summary: The former Japanese Consul General appeared after receiving new orders but again refused the original Allied demands, claiming they exceeded his instructions and disputing the title “former.” Dublin recommends that he be ordered to stop quibbling, surrender bank books and other evidence, and obey Allied representatives, with his funds stopped if necessary.

subfiles.title: Telegram 2851 from Buenos Aires on Japanese funds
subfiles.about: Reports the property transfer and requests detailed instructions for handling more than four million Argentine pesos in Japanese funds.
subfiles.summary: The Allied representatives have taken custody of the property and archives, while a separate protocol will govern cash, bank deposits, private funds, and disputed bonds. The Swiss propose retaining funds for protection work, Japanese personnel, possible repatriation, and transfers elsewhere in South America. Cabot recommends treating the bonds as official funds, withholding salaries from former diplomats, paying internees from private funds, and charging all expenses to Japanese rather than Allied money.

subfiles.title: Telegram 220 from Dublin on the consul’s refusal
subfiles.about: Reports the Japanese Consul General’s return of the Allied memorandum and his proposed alternative transfer procedure.
subfiles.summary: The consul questions whether the Allied representatives understand his instructions, offers to deliver only the property in his own schedule, and asks about passage home. Gray describes his tone as controversial and recommends that Tokyo order immediate, exact compliance and require notice to the American and British missions.

subfiles.title: Outgoing telegram 178 to Dublin
subfiles.about: Reports that MacArthur directed Japan to send urgent instructions to its consul in Dublin.
subfiles.summary: The Department advises that on November 26 MacArthur instructed the Japanese government to issue the stronger directions recommended in Dublin telegram 220. The message thereby confirms action through occupation authorities in Japan.

subfiles.title: Outgoing telegram 2376 to Moscow
subfiles.about: Directs delivery of the omitted MacArthur directive to the Soviet Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: The Department explains that the records-and-property directive was absent from the set furnished to the Soviet Embassy and carried to Moscow by Kennan. It stresses the importance of Soviet receipt because the United States seeks joint action on Japanese records and archives.

subfiles.title: Despatch 2055 on the Dublin consul’s refusal
subfiles.about: Provides a detailed account of the failed attempt to secure Japanese consular archives and property in Dublin.
subfiles.summary: Gray encloses the Allied memorandum, the Japanese response, and newspaper notices about the recall of the consul. He explains that the Japanese side relied on the Allies’ lack of the exact Tokyo instructions, offered an incomplete inventory omitting automobiles, and adopted a face-saving public posture. American and British representatives recommend a forceful order from Tokyo and plan no reply or travel arrangements in the meantime.

subfiles.title: Allied memorandum to the former Japanese Consul General
subfiles.from: Thomas McEnelly and Geoffrey F. Braddock
subfiles.to: Former Japanese Consul General in Dublin
subfiles.about: Summons the consul and specifies the records, keys, assets, and personnel data required for transfer.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum orders the consul to attend a November 12 meeting at the American Consulate General. Its eleven-item list covers recall instructions, leases, automobiles, bank accounts, property, keys, inventories, Japanese residents, and consular employees.

subfiles.title: Japanese Consulate-General memorandum responding to the Allies
subfiles.from: Kazuo Ichihashi for the Japanese Consulate-General, Dublin
subfiles.to: Authorized representative of the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Offers to deliver a limited inventory while requesting travel arrangements for recalled Japanese consular personnel.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese Consulate returns the Allied memorandum because it does not show acceptance of the exact Japanese approach transmitted through a third party. It offers to deliver official property and archives listed in “List A” and asks the Allies to facilitate passage to Tokyo for the personnel named in “List B,” with advance notice of travel dates.

subfiles.title: Dublin newspaper clippings on the recall of Japanese consular personnel
subfiles.from: The Irish Times, The Irish Press, and Irish Independent
subfiles.about: Reports the recall of Setsuya Beppu and Kazuo Ichihashi and the closing of the Japanese consular office.
subfiles.summary: The notices state that the consul general and consul were ordered to report to the Foreign Office in Tokyo and would leave Ireland once travel could be arranged. One account carries the Beppus’ expression of appreciation for their Irish friends and acquaintances.

subfiles.title: Departmental circulation of Despatch 2055
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation; Office of Strategic Services
subfiles.about: Distributes the Dublin despatch on the Japanese consul’s refusal to intelligence agencies.
subfiles.summary: The Department circulates a copy of Despatch 2055 for possible value to four military, naval, investigative, and intelligence offices. The enclosure is identified by its subject concerning refusal to surrender archives and property.

subfiles.title: Despatch 1317 on the transfer in Argentina
subfiles.from: John M. Cabot, American Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Reports the formal transfer of former Japanese diplomatic and consular property and archives in Argentina.
subfiles.summary: Cabot encloses the protocol signed by the British, Swiss, and American representatives and explains the steps leading to the November 13 transfer. He also reports notice to the Argentine Foreign Ministry and plans to move the archives to rented space in the Fortabat Building, where the Swiss would continue routine work for Japanese nationals.

subfiles.title: Protocol transferring Japanese property and archives in Argentina
subfiles.from: Sir David Victor Kelly, Edward Feer, and John Moors Cabot
subfiles.to: Four Allied Powers and Swiss Legation records
subfiles.about: Formally acknowledges Allied receipt of Japanese diplomatic and consular property and archives from Swiss custody.
subfiles.summary: The protocol records that the British and American representatives act for China, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States. It states that the attached inventory was checked and provides that funds and negotiable instruments will be transferred under a separate protocol.

subfiles.title: Inventory of Japanese Embassy furniture and office equipment in Argentina
subfiles.about: Lists furniture, safes, files, typewriters, trunks, and other property belonging to the Japanese Embassy in Argentina.
subfiles.summary: The Spanish-language inventory enumerates more than eighty controlled items, including desks, chairs, filing cabinets, safes, typewriters, bound newspapers, and office fittings. Final entries identify a sealed cabinet, trunks of folders, and twelve numbered wooden boxes, with transfer and receipt annotations dated November 13, 1945.

subfiles.title: American Embassy note to the Swiss Legation
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Swiss order to relinquish Japanese property and archives and outlines immediate Allied possession.
subfiles.summary: The note states that the American and British embassies will receive the material on behalf of the four Allied Powers. It records the understanding that the Swiss will continue routine protection functions for Japanese nationals and diplomatic internees.

subfiles.title: Note verbale to the Argentine Foreign Ministry
subfiles.to: Argentine Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Worship
subfiles.about: Notifies Argentina of the transfer and promises access to the Japanese archives.
subfiles.summary: The note reports that the Swiss relinquished Japanese diplomatic and consular property and archives to the American and British embassies acting for the four Allied Powers. It confirms continued Swiss protection work and offers archive access under Resolution LII of the Inter-American Conference on Problems of War and Peace.

subfiles.title: Despatch 13,036 on depositing Japanese funds in Chile
subfiles.about: Reports temporary bank arrangements for Japanese government bonds and cash taken into Allied custody.
subfiles.summary: The embassy opened safekeeping, checking, and time-deposit accounts at the National City Bank of New York for three million Chilean pesos in bonds and 900,000 pesos in cash. Another 304,544.18 pesos remained with the Swedish Legation for routine protection expenses, and the British and Chinese missions were being informed.

subfiles.title: National City Bank letter acknowledging the cash deposit
subfiles.from: National City Bank of New York, Santiago branch
subfiles.about: Confirms receipt of 900,000 Chilean pesos for the Embassy’s Special Funds Account.
subfiles.summary: The bank acknowledges the deposit made by George D. Andrews. It records the serial numbers of the 10,000-peso notes comprising the funds.

subfiles.title: Bowers letter governing the Japanese fund accounts
subfiles.to: National City Bank of New York, Santiago
subfiles.about: Defines the operation and withdrawal authority for the accounts holding Japanese official funds.
subfiles.summary: Bowers confirms the safekeeping and checking accounts and the Valparaíso time deposit at two percent interest. He directs that bond proceeds enter the checking account and that withdrawals require instructions from the accredited American chief of mission in Chile.

subfiles.title: Custody receipt 6737 for Chilean bonds
subfiles.from: National City Bank of New York, Santiago
subfiles.to: Embassy of the United States of America Special Funds Account
subfiles.about: Acknowledges safekeeping of Japanese-held Chilean bonds with a total nominal value of three million pesos.
subfiles.summary: The receipt itemizes internal Chilean debt, Caja de Crédito Hipotecario, and Banco Hipotecario de Valparaíso bonds. It records quantities, serial ranges, coupon dates, and redemption dates for each issue.

subfiles.title: Bank acknowledgment of Bowers’s account instructions
subfiles.from: National City Bank of New York, Santiago branch
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the ambassador’s instructions and encloses a receipt for the 900,000-peso time deposit.
subfiles.summary: The bank confirms that it has noted the controls governing the Special Funds Account. It encloses safekeeping receipt 6745 for the time deposit.

subfiles.title: Despatch 13,047 on delivery of Japanese property and archives in Chile
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, American Embassy, Santiago
subfiles.about: Reports the Swedish transfer of Japanese property, archives, and funds to Bowers as representative of the Allied Powers.
subfiles.summary: Bowers describes receipt of a Japanese-resident register, documents including the former minister’s diary and reports on American war industries, three million pesos in bonds, and 900,000 pesos in cash. Much property would remain temporarily in the Swedish chancery, but the embassy anticipated transport and storage expenses after July 1, 1946. Because the Chinese Legation lacked adequate Japanese-language capacity, Bowers recommends sending the archives to Washington for examination.

subfiles.title: Wennerberg note offering Japanese property to the Allies
subfiles.about: Offers to transfer Japanese diplomatic and consular property held by the Swedish Legation to a jointly selected Allied representative.
subfiles.summary: Wennerberg reports instructions received through Sweden after a request from the Japanese Minister in Stockholm. He asks whether Bowers and his British and Chinese colleagues will appoint a recipient and seeks consent to continue routine protection of Japanese citizens in Chile.

subfiles.title: Bowers reply accepting Japanese property
subfiles.about: Accepts custody on behalf of the Allied Powers and approves continued Swedish protection work.
subfiles.summary: Bowers states that his British and Chinese colleagues have authorized him to receive the Japanese government property, there being no Soviet diplomatic official in Chile. He raises no objection to the Swedish Legation’s continuation of routine work for Japanese subjects.

subfiles.title: British Embassy reply designating Bowers
subfiles.about: Confirms British agreement that Bowers receive the property and that Sweden continue Japanese protection work.
subfiles.summary: The British ambassador agrees to joint custody for the Allied Powers in the absence of a Soviet representative. He designates Claude G. Bowers as the receiving representative and approves continued Swedish routine protection of Japanese subjects.

subfiles.title: Chinese Legation reply designating Bowers
subfiles.about: Authorizes the American ambassador to receive Japanese property for the Allied Powers.
subfiles.summary: Tang Wu acknowledges Wennerberg’s note concerning the property held for the former Japanese minister. He states that he and the British ambassador have asked Bowers to act as their representative.

subfiles.title: Memorandum recording the Chilean transfer
subfiles.from: Folke Wennerberg and Claude G. Bowers
subfiles.about: Records the transfer of Japanese archives, records, bonds, and cash from Swedish to Allied custody.
subfiles.summary: Wennerberg transfers an inventory, Special Box No. 7, a register of Japanese subjects, three million pesos in Chilean bonds, and 900,000 pesos in cash. The Swedish Legation retains 304,544.18 pesos for protection expenses and agrees to deliver the remaining physical property when convenient.

subfiles.title: Swedish Legation statement of Japanese funds
subfiles.about: Accounts for Japanese cash, bonds, bank funds, and expenditures administered by the Swedish Legation.
subfiles.summary: The Spanish-language statement compares the funds received in March 1943 with balances held on November 5, 1945. It records total holdings of 4,204,544.18 pesos after expenses of 295,455.82 pesos.

subfiles.title: Exchange of letters transferring Japanese funds to Swedish custody
subfiles.about: Documents Sweden’s receipt of Japanese government banknotes and bonds in Chile.
subfiles.summary: Yamagata delivers 1.5 million Chilean pesos in banknotes and three million pesos in specified bonds to the Swedish representative responsible for Japanese interests. Wennerberg confirms that the funds and securities were counted and received on March 10, 1943.

subfiles.title: Schedules of Chilean banknotes and bonds
subfiles.about: Lists serial numbers and identifying details for Japanese-owned Chilean banknotes and securities.
subfiles.summary: The first schedule records the serial numbers of Banco Central de Chile 10,000-peso notes. The second identifies Caja Hipotecaria, Banco Hipotecario de Valparaíso, and Chilean internal-debt bonds totaling three million pesos, together with coupon information.

subfiles.title: Inventory of the Japanese Legation in Chile
subfiles.about: Catalogues furniture, furnishings, appliances, vehicles, and household effects belonging to the Japanese Legation in Chile.
subfiles.summary: The inventory lists tables, chairs, cabinets, artworks, ornaments, safes, clocks, typewriters, carpets, a piano, radios, beds, garden tools, mirrors, appliances, and lamps, often cross-referenced to photographs. It also notes that a Buick automobile was sold on November 10, 1943. The inventory continues beyond page 160.
